When to Charge: Free as Strategy or Avoidance

Should we charge yet — and is free a strategy or avoidance?

1. A Monday morning in Bengaluru

At 9:40 a.m. on 14 September 2026, Rhea Kapoor opened the board deck for Purvai Labs on her laptop in a Koramangala meeting room and reread the second slide for the fourth time that morning. Purvai Labs made an AI doubt-solving app for students preparing for board exams and entrance tests — type or photograph a problem, get a worked explanation back in under ten seconds, in Hindi or English, from a tutor built on top of a large language model. It had 5,00,000 monthly active users, almost none of them paying anything, and eighteen months of runway that had just become six.

The number that had triggered the meeting was not user growth, which was fine — up 14% quarter over quarter — nor retention, which was respectable for an education app: 38% of new users were still opening it thirty days later. The number was ₹3.2 crore, the company's new monthly burn, up from ₹2.1 crore nine months earlier, because the AI model calls that answered every doubt now cost more per student than they used to. Purvai's seed investors, sitting across the table, wanted an answer to one question before they'd discuss the next cheque: was free a strategy Rhea could defend with evidence, or was it something the founding team had backed into because nobody wanted to be the one who put a price tag on helping a sixteen-year-old with algebra homework. Six months of cash concentrates a founder's mind wonderfully on the difference.

2. The idea, plainly stated

"When to charge" is a decision about timing: at what point does a product stop giving away the thing it does for free and start asking for money for some or all of it. It sits downstream of two other questions a team must already have answers to — what the revenue model even is (advertising, subscription, transaction fee, or something else), and what interview and usage evidence says about whether anyone would pay at all. Given those two inputs, the timing question asks something narrower and more operational: not can we charge, but should we, now, given what staying free costs us and what we actually know.

The distinction the learning objective points at — free as strategy versus free as avoidance — was not handed down by a single named academic the way, say, discounted cash flow was. It crystallised through the 2010s and 2020s out of two overlapping traditions: Chris Anderson's 2009 book Free, which argued that giving a product away could be a deliberate, calculated business decision rather than a concession, and a harder-nosed pricing-consultancy tradition — visible in Madhavan Ramanujam's 2016 Monetizing Innovation and in the operating playbooks of freemium software companies like Dropbox, Slack and Zoom — which insisted that "free" needs the same rigour as any other pricing decision, with a hypothesis, a metric, and a date by which the hypothesis gets tested. The sentence Rhea could say in that boardroom without sounding glib is this one: free is a strategy when it is bought deliberately, with a specific piece of evidence in mind and a date by which you'll have it; it is avoidance when it persists because nobody has decided otherwise. The test is not how long you've been free. It's whether you can name, right now, the evidence you're still waiting on and what it will cost you to wait for it.

3. How the timing decision actually gets made

Practitioners who are good at this rarely reason from a single number. They separate the question into steps, several of which are usually left implicit and only surface when someone forces them into the open, which is exactly what Purvai's board did.

Step one: name the actual reason you are free. There are at least three distinct legitimate reasons, and they call for different tests. You might be free because the marginal cost of serving one more user is close to zero and the value of scale (network effects, word of mouth, brand) outweighs the forgone revenue — that's free-for-distribution. You might be free because you don't yet know if anyone would pay and can't afford to guess wrong — that's free-for-evidence. Or you might be free because customers have come to expect it and switching them to paid risks losing them to a rival who stays free longer — free-for-lock-in. Purvai's team, when pressed, realised they had drifted from the second reason into something closer to inertia: the evidence-gathering they'd told themselves they were doing eighteen months ago had, in practice, stopped about a year ago.

Step two: price the cost of staying free. This is the step teams skip most often, because it requires totalling up marginal cost per free user — infrastructure, support, and, for an AI product, inference cost — and multiplying by the free base, then asking whether that number is shrinking, flat, or growing as a share of burn. A traditional SaaS product's marginal cost per user is close to zero and roughly constant; an LLM-based product's marginal cost per user moves with model choice and with how deeply each user engages, and it can rise sharply even while the user base holds still.

Step three: separate stated willingness to pay from revealed willingness to pay. An interview answer ("yes, I'd pay ₹299 a month for that") is a claim; a completed transaction is a fact. Good teams treat the interview evidence as a reason to run a real test — a soft paywall on a slice of traffic, a waitlist with a card required, a limited-time offer — rather than as sufficient evidence on its own.

Step four: set a tripwire before you need one. This means choosing, in advance and while calm, the specific number or date that will trigger a pricing decision regardless of how the team feels in the moment — for instance, "if cost-to-serve exceeds 55% of burn, or 1 October, whichever comes first, we introduce a cap." Without a tripwire, the decision keeps getting made by default, which is another way of saying it isn't being made at all.

4. Working the numbers, twice

Rhea's team had two pieces of interview evidence sitting in a shared document nobody had opened since March. Forty power users — the top 5% by weekly sessions — had been asked if they'd pay ₹299 a month for an unlimited-doubts tier once the free plan capped out; 26 of 40, or 65%, said yes. A broader survey of 2,000 users representative of the full base found only 9% willing at that price. That gap between power-user enthusiasm and average-user indifference is itself a finding, not a nuisance to average away.

Here is the arithmetic the board wanted walked through line by line. Purvai's top decile by usage — the students who open the app most often — was 10% of 5,00,000 monthly active users, or 50,000 people. If a realistic 8% of that decile converted to the ₹299 tier once it existed, that's 4,000 paying users. Revenue: 4,000 × ₹299 = ₹11,96,000, call it ₹12 lakh a month. Total monthly burn was ₹3.2 crore. ₹12 lakh against ₹3.2 crore is 3.75% of burn covered — on its own, nowhere near survival, but not nothing either. It would trim effective burn to about ₹3.08 crore, which against ₹19.2 crore in the bank stretches runway from 6.0 months to roughly 6.2 months. A week of extra runway is not what saves a company. What it does is convert "we think people would pay" into "125 users out of 50,000 did," which is the kind of fact a board can build a plan around.

In the cost-shock case, patience costs a month and a half of runway, and the only defensible move is to cap the free tier immediately — independent of whether ₹299 turns out to be the right price — because the free product itself has become the emergency. One input changing the marginal cost of service turned a research question into a solvency question.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

Free-for-distribution is not free-for-evidence

Both look identical from the outside — a product with no price tag — but they answer to different clocks. A distribution play stays free until network effects or brand strength are strong enough that charging won't undo them; an evidence play stays free only until the specific question it was meant to answer has been answered. Conflating the two is how "we're still gathering data" survives two years after the data stopped changing.

Stated willingness to pay overstates itself

People are agreeable in interviews, especially about a product they already like for free. The 65% of Purvai's power users who said yes to ₹299 is a real and useful signal, but it is not a forecast; it is a reason to run the soft-paywall test that produces an actual conversion rate, which is usually a fraction of the stated number.

Freemium is a family, not one lever

A usage cap (ten free doubts a day), a feature gate (step-by-step explanations are paid, final answers are free), and a time-boxed trial (thirty days of everything, then a wall) test different things and are different degrees of reversible. A cap is easy to loosen if conversion disappoints; a trial that has already ended is hard to un-end without looking erratic to the very users you're trying to convert.

Retention proves value, not price

Purvai's 38% D30 retention says the product is worth opening again. It says nothing about what anyone would pay for that value, because "worth using when it's free" and "worth ₹299 a month" are separate claims tested by separate evidence. Teams that treat strong retention as proof they're ready to charge are answering a question nobody asked.

The fear of losing growth is usually untested and usually about the wrong users

Every team worries a paywall will tank growth. What actually happens, most of the time, is that the users who leave are disproportionately the ones who were never going to convert or refer anyone — the growth lost is often the least valuable kind, and the fear is rarely checked against a real cohort before it's used to justify indefinite delay.

Marginal cost is not a constant for AI products

Classic software pricing theory assumes the cost of serving one more free user is near zero and stays there, which is why "free forever, monetise later" worked for so much of consumer internet history. An LLM-based product breaks that assumption twice over: cost per call is non-trivial, and it can rise on its own as usage deepens or as the underlying model is upgraded, with no change in user count at all. Free has an expiry clock here that pure software never had.

Platform and payment mechanics add lead time you must plan for

In India, a consumer subscription has to work inside Google Play's billing rules and, for recurring debits, the RBI's e-mandate framework via UPI Autopay, which requires advance user notification before each renewal. None of that is a pricing decision, but all of it adds real weeks between "we've decided to charge" and "we're collecting money," which means the tripwire has to fire earlier than the cash-out-date it's protecting against.

The model tells you when, not how much or how

Everything above helps decide whether to keep a product free or start charging. It does not tell you what to charge, which features belong in which tier, or how to price-discriminate between a school student and a working professional using the same app. Those are packaging and pricing-architecture questions, and answering the timing question well is a precondition for asking them properly, not a substitute for asking them at all.

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products, the trigger tends to be a habit-formation curve: teams watch D30 and D90 retention flatten, treat the flattening as a sign the product's value has stabilised, and start paywall testing around that point, the way Duolingo built years of a free tier before layering Super Duolingo on top once daily-habit data was strong, or the way Dropbox — Chris Anderson's favourite example — gave away storage until the cost of the heaviest users made the free ceiling worth defending. In B2B software, the picture is different because fully free is rare and usually temporary: a trial has an expiry date from day one, and the willingness-to-pay evidence comes not from surveys but from a champion inside the customer walking a procurement conversation through an ROI number, so "when to charge" is less about population-level conversion and more about whether one deal's math holds up, which is closer to how Slack moved workspaces from free to paid seats once message-history limits started to bind real teams. In marketplaces, the question usually isn't whether to charge but which side: one side — often the side that's scarcer or harder to attract, frequently buyers — stays free indefinitely to keep liquidity high, while the other side pays, and the timing decision becomes about how much liquidity is enough before asking the paying side to pay more, not whether to charge at all.

Stage matters too. An early-stage company like Purvai is burning investor cash to buy evidence and has weak leverage — a "free forever" promise made carelessly in year one is expensive to walk back once users have built workflows around it, and doing so publicly can cost more in goodwill than the revenue is worth. A large, established company has richer usage data and can price-discriminate with more precision across segments, but carries a different risk: raising a price on a captured base reads as a betrayal rather than a discovery, which is why price increases at scale get rolled out gradually, grandfathered, and explained, rather than sprung on users the way an early paywall test can be.

7. Common mistakes

Mistaking growth for demand

Symptom: DAU keeps climbing while average session depth stays flat or falls. Misunderstanding: usage is being read as proof of value intense enough to pay for, when it may just mean the product is easy to open and free. Cheapest diagnostic: run a soft paywall on a small random slice of traffic and see whether depth-of-use, not just headcount, predicts who converts.

Pricing only when the CFO panics

Symptom: a paywall gets announced abruptly, days after a fundraising round falls through or a board meeting turns tense. Misunderstanding: treating pricing as an emergency lever rather than a hypothesis that should have had a test date months earlier. Cheapest diagnostic: ask whether a written pricing hypothesis with a date predates the crisis; if it doesn't exist, the team was practising avoidance, not patience.

Overfitting the price to power users

Symptom: the launch price is set from the enthusiastic top 5%, and the broader base churns hard when the wall goes up. Misunderstanding: mistaking the loudest, most engaged segment for the representative one. Cheapest diagnostic: cut every willingness-to-pay result by usage decile before setting a number, exactly as the 65%-versus-9% split at Purvai should have been read from the start.

No tripwire, indefinite free

Symptom: "we'll revisit monetisation next quarter" appears in four consecutive quarterly reviews with no new evidence attached. Misunderstanding: treating timing as a feeling that will eventually feel right, rather than a testable claim with a falsification date. Cheapest diagnostic: ask the team to name the exact number that would flip them to "charge now" and the date by which they expect to see it; silence is the answer.

8. What good looks like

Ninety days after that board meeting, Purvai had not tried to answer the pricing-level question and the timing question at once, which is the trap most teams fall into under pressure. Rhea's team first capped the free tier at ten doubts a day — a cost-control move, made immediately, independent of what price would eventually work — and only then rolled out the ₹299 unlimited tier to a randomly selected 20% of the base, holding the rest as a comparison group. Six weeks in, the paying share of that slice was 4.6% of the top usage decile, close enough to the 8% assumption to be credible and far enough below the 65% interview number to confirm that stated intent had inflated the estimate roughly seven-fold, a gap now written down as a standing calibration factor for every future pricing test. Each tier was built so its price covered its own inference cost with margin left over, which is the kind of teardown exercise pricing courses at Kellogg and NUS build around real companies' historical price changes: work backward from unit economics to the price, not forward from a number that feels fair. The board got a slide with a conversion rate instead of a survey result, and Purvai got eleven weeks of extra runway it could point to and defend.

9. What Rhea decided, and two questions to sit with

Rhea recommended, and the board accepted, an immediate usage cap to control cost, paired with a phased paywall test rather than a full launch — because the evidence said value was real (retention, session depth, the power-user interviews) but incomplete (the wide gap to the average-user survey, and no revealed-preference data yet), while the cost curve said waiting for that evidence to mature on its own timetable was no longer affordable. That is the shape of a well-made timing decision: it treats the cost of staying free and the maturity of the willingness-to-pay evidence as two separate readings, and it acts on whichever one is more urgent rather than waiting for both to agree.

The next stop from here is packaging: once you know a product is ready to charge, how do you split one price into tiers that route a school student, a coaching-centre reseller, and an anxious parent each to the plan suited to what they'd actually pay — because timing tells you when to open the door, not how many rooms to put behind it.

Two questions worth sitting with. First: if the marginal cost of serving your product free stayed at zero forever, would you still choose to start charging — and if the honest answer is yes, what is that decision actually protecting? Second: what specific number, if it appeared on your dashboard tomorrow morning, would be enough to move you from "not yet" to "now" — and if you cannot name it today, what does that tell you about how the decision is actually being made?

Vaakya Voice Cloud: The Price of Free

A decision case in Go-to-Market, Growth and Monetisation (Pricing and Packaging)

1. Opening

On Sunday, 18 October 2026, a little after ten at night, Jayashree Vaidya was still at the dining table of her flat in Baner, Pune, two laptops open and the tea gone cold. The board of Vaakya Voice Cloud met at nine the next morning, and the pre-read she had circulated carried a slide titled "Dealer monetisation: recommendation" with nothing under the heading but a placeholder rectangle. Her co-founder had noticed, and had sent one line at 9.14 p.m.: "Jaya, the rectangle. Tomorrow."

Vaakya sold AI voice agents that answered after-sales calls in eleven Indian languages. Twenty-one consumer brands paid for it; forty thousand small service centres used it every month and paid nothing. The term sheet from Jyotirmay Capital expired on 31 October, thirteen days away, and carried a covenant Jayashree could recite: monthly revenue of at least ₹30 lakh from the dealer side by 31 March 2027. Nobody at Vaakya had ever charged a dealer a rupee.

The question on the slide was whether to start. Underneath it was a harder one she had not found a way to phrase for a board: whether the free tier was the machine that made the paid side work, or a habit the company had stopped examining because examining it was costly.

2. Company history

Vaakya Voice Cloud was founded in Pune in March 2022 by Vikramaditya Jagtap, who had run service operations for a two-wheeler manufacturer in Nagpur, and two speech engineers from Bengaluru. The founding observation was mundane and correct: when a washing machine fails in Jalgaon or a scooter will not start in Warangal, the customer calls the nearest authorised service point, and that point is three people, one landline and a register. Calls go unanswered; the brand never learns.

Vaakya's agent picked up, took the complaint in the caller's language, checked warranty status, booked a slot and wrote the record into the brand's service system. The first contract, with the durables maker Vasundhara Durables, was signed in September 2023 and priced per AI-handled minute, because minutes were what telephony vendors billed and nobody wanted to argue a new unit in a first contract.

One earlier decision shaped everything available in October 2026. In June 2024, choosing between building its own speech stack and licensing a commercial one, the company licensed. The reasoning remains defensible: it bought eighteen months of speed, it let Vaakya add Tamil, Telugu and Bengali in a single quarter, and it meant twelve engineers instead of forty. The consequence is a cost of goods Vaakya does not control, denominated per second of audio: every free minute is a real payment to a supplier. In January 2025, with that cost believed small, the company opened the free Vaakya Jan tier to any service centre in the country, whether or not its brand was a customer. Growth followed. So did the bill.

3. The industry

The Indian customer-support software market in 2026 was neither empty nor settled. Freshworks and Zoho Desk owned the ticketing layer and sold per agent seat. Yellow.ai, Haptik and Gupshup sold chat and voice bots to enterprises on annual contracts. Exotel and Ozonetel supplied the telephony underneath, and Sarvam AI and others had made Indian-language speech models better and cheaper each year. All sold to the brand, not the dealer, and none cared whether a two-person workshop in Solapur answered its phone.

That gap was Vaakya's position and its problem. Its supply of coverage came from small businesses with no software budget and often no card on file; its demand came from brands buying that coverage. Regulation touched both sides. Outbound calling ran through TRAI's registered-telemarketer framework, and from 2024 the Digital Personal Data Protection Act forced Vaakya to re-paper consent for every recorded call, a project that took most of a quarter and produced a consent screen in two of the eleven languages.

Exposure was not only domestic. The largest contract by value was with Jazeera Appliance Trading LLC of Dubai, which distributed Indian-made appliances across the Gulf and used Vaakya in Arabic, Malayalam and Hindi. The data scientist sat in Toronto, the design lead in Berlin and the enterprise sales head in New Jersey, a spread cheap to assemble in 2023 and now taking a disproportionate share of a payroll denominated in rupees.

Figure A. Vaakya Voice Cloud, 2022 to 2026.

4. The situation in detail

For most of 2025 the internal number for the cost of a free minute was ₹0.90. It appeared in a growth memo, then a board deck, then the plan that justified opening the Jan tier to non-customer brands. It came from one week in October 2024, before Tamil, Telugu and Bengali launched and before the supplier moved from whole minutes to billed seconds with a per-session charge. Nobody revisited it because nobody owned it.

In March 2026 a finance review, prompted by a bank reconciliation rather than by product, rebuilt the figure from invoices. The blended cost of a free-tier minute was ₹2.00, not ₹0.90, and the shape underneath was counter-intuitive: the heaviest users were cheapest per minute, because their calls batched well and amortised the session charge, while centres taking a handful of short calls a month were the most expensive. Exhibit 1 sets this out. Free-tier minutes cost ₹72.80 lakh in August 2026 against ₹124.80 lakh of enterprise revenue: 58 per cent of everything the brands paid went to serving people who paid nothing.

Three further beliefs have come apart. The first was that free-tier centres were a funnel into paid enterprise coverage; in practice brands bought coverage first and then asked Vaakya to enrol their service points, so the causality ran the other way. The second was that the product worked: the dashboard said so — Exhibit 4 reports a resolution rate of 76.6 per cent for August — but a hand audit of 600 calls, in Exhibit 5, put clean resolution at 53.0 per cent. The third was that the July pilot would settle the price question. It did not, for reasons Exhibit 6 shows only if the footnote is read.

5. The people

Jayashree Vaidya, Chief Product Officer, Pune, joined in 2024 from a payments company. Her position is that Vaakya should charge dealers "when we can defend the number", which has satisfied nobody for two quarters. Her incentive is a Series B that vests a tranche of her options. She has not said aloud that she believes Exhibit 5 over Exhibit 4, and is uneasy about pricing a product that, on the audit's count, gives the caller wrong information in 54 of 600 calls.

Vikramaditya Jagtap, co-founder and Chief Executive, Pune, wants a dealer revenue line before 31 October, arguing with some justice that a company which has never asked its users for money cannot know they value it. His incentive is the term sheet and his dilution. He has not told the team that on 6 October he described the metered plan to Jyotirmay Capital as "going live in November".

Jaswinder Virk, Head of Growth, Gurugram, is against charging before the festive peak. His target is 60,000 active centres by March. He points out, correctly, that no competitor is signing up small workshops, and that charging would end that. He has not volunteered that roughly a fifth of the active base was onboarded by his own field team under a per-signup incentive and makes fewer than five calls a month.

Vaishnavi Jog, Staff Data Scientist, Toronto, designed the July pilot and is most insistent it cannot bear the weight put on it. Her fully loaded cost is a little under three and a half times a senior Pune engineer's, raised at every budget review. She has not told the team that a fourth arm was run and dropped: 2,000 centres were offered a ₹1,499 plan and 14 took it, a take-up of 0.7 per cent. She removed it expecting it to be quoted as proof that dealers never pay.

Jonas Vollmer, Design Lead, Berlin, argues that per-minute pricing is indefensible to a dealer, who then pays more when the agent is slow, and that any charge must be metered against a unit the dealer recognises as value. He has not told the chief executive that the billing and consent screens exist in English and Hindi only, and that shipping nine more languages before November is not something he would commit to.

Vandana Jayaram, Customer Success Lead, Singapore, ran the 600-call audit over eleven days. Her position is that price follows quality, not the reverse; her bonus depends on renewals. She has not put in writing that two of the three anchors have already asked informally for a lower rate, citing the audit she circulated.

Jerome Vaz, Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey, calls the dealer question a distraction and wants the blended enterprise rate raised from ₹6.50 to ₹8.00 a minute at renewal, adding ₹28.80 lakh a month on August volumes. He is paid on contract value. He has not flagged that the two largest names in his pipeline are evaluating a competitor.

Javed Vakharia, Group Service Head, Jazeera Appliance Trading LLC, Dubai, is the largest account. He will renew on 31 December only with a service-credit clause tied to resolution quality in Arabic and Malayalam. He has not mentioned that his board has asked him to cut the group's software vendors.

7. Voices

"I am not against charging. I am against charging on Tuesday for something we audited on Thursday. If a dealer pays ₹499 and the agent tells his customer the warranty has lapsed when it has not, he does not churn quietly. He tells the WhatsApp group."

Vandana Jayaram, leadership call, 12 October

"Arm C is not a result, it is a coincidence with a good haircut. Gujarat in July is a different month from Karnataka in July. Put arm C on a board slide and I will ask for my name to come off the deck."

Vaishnavi Jog, in the pilot review thread, 14 October

"Every quarter we say the funnel is not ready, and every month we pay ₹72.80 lakh to answer telephones for people we have never once asked for anything. At some point 'not yet' is just a decision made badly."

Vikramaditya Jagtap, board pre-read email, 16 October

"Sir, the machine is good, no problem. But ₹3 per minute, and it takes four minutes to understand my customer's Marathi? I should pay for its slowness? Give me a rate per complaint closed, I will pay happily."

Proprietor, two-wheeler service point, Kolhapur, pilot exit call, 6 August

"I want to be clear with you before December. Price is not my problem. Arabic and Malayalam are my problem. Fix those and I will discuss price with you as a friend."

Javed Vakharia, renewal call, 9 October

8. The options as Jayashree currently sees them

Option 1: meter the free tier from 1 November. Sixty minutes free, then ₹3 a minute: the arm C design. On arm C's own ₹71.04 of revenue per centre shown, across all 40,000 active centres, this yields ₹28.42 lakh a month, which is 39.0 per cent of the free tier's ₹72.80 lakh cost and still short of the ₹30 lakh covenant. On arm C's stop rate of 9.0 per cent it also loses about 3,600 centres. Jaswinder's objection is not the size of the money but its timing.

Option 2: hold free, ship the in-house model, revisit in April. The Bengaluru team's own stack, Varnmala version three, would cut the free-tier cost per minute from ₹2.00 to an estimated ₹0.95, saving ₹38.22 lakh a month, cutting the operating loss to ₹95.78 lakh and stretching runway to about nineteen and a half months. The date has slipped twice, and the model is strongest in Hindi, Marathi and Gujarati, already the cheapest and best-served; the expensive minutes are Tamil, Telugu and Bengali.

Option 3: leave dealers alone and reprice the brands. Jerome's plan, ₹8.00 a minute blended at renewal, adds ₹28.80 lakh a month on August volumes, which covers 28.80 of the 134.00 lakh operating loss, or 21.5 per cent of it, not most of the gap in Exhibit 3. Against it: two of the three anchors have signalled they want less, not more, and the anchors carry the coverage undertakings.

All three options take the minute as the unit, because the telephony vendor bills minutes and the 2023 contract copied it. The Kolhapur proprietor, Jonas and Javed have each said in different words that the unit is wrong — that what both sides buy is a complaint closed, and Vaakya has never priced the thing it sells. A fourth framing is on nobody's slide: Vaakya has two customers and has never chosen between them, and the coverage undertakings answered that question already, on terms the company did not negotiate.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Cash of ₹18.76 crore at 30 September and an operating loss of ₹134.00 lakh a month give fourteen months: long enough that haste is unnecessary, short enough that drift is irresponsible. The Jyotirmay Capital term sheet, ₹92 crore at a ₹460 crore pre-money valuation, expires on 31 October and carries the dealer-revenue covenant. The reserved-GPU commitment of ₹14.40 lakh a month runs to 30 June 2027 whether the minutes are used or not, so roughly ₹58.40 lakh of the free tier's cost is genuinely variable.

The three anchor contracts require Vaakya to be live at no fewer than 85 per cent of each brand's authorised service points. For Vasundhara Durables, 10,032 of 11,400 points are live, or 88.0 per cent, and 8,600 of those sit on the free tier. If arm C's stop rate held, about 774 would go dark, leaving 9,258 of 11,400 live: 81.2 per cent, and still a breach. Regulation adds two edges: billing a dealer requires a GST invoice and a consent flow that exists in two languages, and the DPDP Act's rules on recorded voice apply equally to free and paid calls, so charging reduces no obligation. There is also a hiring freeze, a support team of four, and a peak that begins the week the board wants the meter switched on.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, say who the free tier subsidises and by how much. Which cohort would you most want to keep if the others were free to lose?
  2. Exhibit 4 and Exhibit 5 disagree about the same product in the same quarter. Reconstruct how each was produced, and decide which you would show the board.
  3. Exhibit 6 makes arm C the winner on both revenue and retention. List every reason that comparison may be invalid, and say what the omitted fourth arm changes about your reading of the pilot.
  4. Vaakya prices in minutes because a telephony vendor did in 2023. What would a price per complaint closed do to Exhibits 2 and 3, and to the argument between Jerome and Vandana? What would it require the company to measure?
  5. The covenant asks for ₹30 lakh of monthly dealer revenue; the best-supported estimate is ₹28.42 lakh, won at the cost of a probable breach of the coverage undertakings. Is a covenant that forces this trade a reason to accept the term sheet, renegotiate it, or decline it? Argue the case you find least comfortable.
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Jayashree put under the heading, what evidence does she show, what does she refuse to commit to, and how does she answer a director who asks, in the first two minutes, whether free has been a strategy or an excuse?

Late on Sunday

At twenty past eleven Jayashree typed three headings — meter, wait, reprice — and beneath them a fourth line she did not know what to do with: we have never asked the brands to pay for coverage as coverage. Vandana's audit sat in one window, the dashboard in the other, both describing August, neither describing the same company. The phone buzzed with a message from Bengaluru about the Varnmala evaluation run, which had finished, and which she decided not to open until morning. The rectangle was still empty.

Tijori Invoicing Cloud: When to Charge

A decision case in Go-to-Market, Growth and Monetisation (Pricing and Packaging)

1. Opening

On the evening of Monday, 5 October 2026, Gitanjali Tambe sat in the Pune office of Tijori Invoicing Cloud with three documents open on her screen: a usage table, a pilot report and a board note that was still blank under the heading "Pricing recommendation". The board would meet at the Indore head office on Friday, 9 October. Diwali fell on 8 November, and every small trader in Tijori's base was about to enter the busiest four weeks of the year. Whatever Gitanjali, the head of product, recommended on Friday would reach those traders before the festival.

The question sounded simple. Tijori had given its product away for two years. Should it start charging now, or was "free" still a growth strategy, and had it perhaps become a way of avoiding an uncomfortable conversation with customers?

2. Company background

Tijori Invoicing Cloud was founded in Indore in 2024 by Gayatri Tendulkar, a chartered accountant, and two engineers. The product helps small traders and manufacturers with annual turnover of ₹1 crore to ₹20 crore to raise GST-compliant invoices, generate e-way bills and, once a business crosses the ₹5 crore turnover threshold, produce e-invoices through the government's invoice registration portal. Its users are wholesalers in Surat, auto-parts dealers in Ludhiana and packaging units in Coimbatore.

The market is crowded and largely free at the entry level. Zoho Invoice and Vyapar offer free plans, myBillBook and Khatabook chase the same shopkeeper, and TallyPrime remains the default for accountants who prefer a desktop. Tijori launched on 14 October 2024 with a free plan, raised a seed round of ₹18 crore in January 2025, and reached 5,00,000 registered users by September 2026. In March 2026 it added e-way bills and e-invoicing to the free plan, partly to match competitors and partly to win larger traders.

Figure A. Key dates in Tijori's first two years and the decision window.

3. The situation

Of the 5,00,000 registered accounts, 2,00,000 were active in September 2026. Exhibit 1 divides them by monthly invoice volume. Light users, who raise fewer than ten invoices a month, made up 60 per cent of the active base and cost about ₹4 each per month to serve, mostly in storage and messaging. Heavy users, who raise fifty or more invoices and run e-way bill and e-invoice calls against government portals, were 10 per cent of the base but cost ₹40 each. Across the whole active base, Tijori spent ₹20.0 lakh a month on infrastructure, an average of ₹10 per active user.

In August, Gitanjali's team ran two four-week pilots on 10,000 Regular and Heavy users, split into two arms of 5,000. One arm saw a paywall at ₹300 a month, the other at ₹500. The team had also surveyed 400 users from the same tiers. Exhibit 2 sets what people said against what they did.

4. The people

Gayatri Tendulkar, chief executive in Indore, wanted revenue on the board slide before the Series A discussions. She was not attached to any particular price but disliked a plan whose end date nobody could name.

Tarun Goyal, head of growth in Gurugram, wanted to stay free through Diwali. New registrations were running at 25,000 a month and the festival season was his best chance to reach 6,00,000 accounts. He read any paywall as an invitation for Vyapar and Zoho to pick up his users.

Tripti Gowda, data scientist in Toronto, wanted the decision framed by evidence. She had rebuilt the pilot twice to make the two arms comparable, and she warned that four weeks could not reveal churn in month three.

Tarini Gopalan, customer-success lead in Singapore, spoke to the largest accounts. Several Heavy users, including a Surat textile trader, had told her they were surprised the product was free and would gladly pay if support improved. Her worry was different: a sudden paywall in Diwali week would flood a four-person support team. Tobias Grunewald, the designer in Berlin, had drafted a gentle upgrade screen but cautioned that it was only as fair as the limit behind it.

Option A: stay free through Diwali. Tijori would hold off until December and use the festival to grow. The upside is the largest possible seasonal intake and no support strain. The cost is that Exhibit 3 shows twelve months of runway and no revenue, and December is only a new date with the same uncertainty. Nothing in the company defined what result would end the free period.

Option B: charge Regular and Heavy users. Light users would stay free, with up to nine invoices a month, while e-way bills, e-invoicing and higher volumes moved to a ₹300 plan, Tijori Plus. Existing users would receive sixty days of full access under a programme called Tarakki Pass. At the pilot's 17 per cent conversion, 13,600 of 80,000 would pay, producing ₹40.8 lakh a month, more than double the ₹20.0 lakh infrastructure bill, and lifting runway to about eighteen months. The cost is a difficult Diwali for support and the risk that pilot conversion falls once the novelty fades.

Option C: charge everyone. All users would pay ₹300 from 1 November. Exhibit 3 looks best here, with runway near twenty-seven months, but the 8 per cent conversion is a guess, since no Light user ever saw a paywall. Tarun estimated that registrations would fall from 25,000 to 9,000 a month, a 64 per cent drop, and that 1,20,000 Light users, the source of most future Regular users, would move to free competitors.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, what does each tier cost Tijori, and which tiers does free serve as marketing rather than subsidy?
  2. What does Exhibit 2 tell you about the difference between stated and revealed willingness to pay, and why might revenue per user shown be more useful than conversion alone?
  3. Exhibit 3 favours Option C on runway. What information is missing from that row, and how should Gitanjali treat an estimate that no pilot has tested?
  4. What test would distinguish "free as a strategy" from "free as avoidance" at Tijori, and does Option A pass it?

7. A note for the learner

This case turns on one distinction. Free is a strategy when it has a purpose, a measured cost and a condition that ends it. It is avoidance when the company cannot say what result would make it charge. Two inputs from the topic graph frame the decision. The revenue model says a price exists somewhere in the product, and interview and pilot evidence says whether anyone will actually pay. Tijori has both: Exhibit 2 shows real payment at two prices.

A well-reasoned answer separates the users whom free helps from the users whom free merely subsidises. Light users cost ₹4.8 lakh a month in total and feed the funnel, since 57,600 of the 80,000 Regular and Heavy users began as Light. Regular and Heavy users cost ₹15.2 lakh a month, use the government-portal features that carry the highest cost, and have demonstrated payment.

One defensible path is Option B. It keeps the top of the funnel that Option C would damage, and it stops the subsidy that Option A prolongs. Choose ₹300, not ₹500, because it yields slightly more revenue per user shown and more paying customers to learn from. Protect the launch: begin the sixty-day Tarakki Pass on 15 October, so payments start after Diwali and support is not flooded, and give the four-person support team temporary help from Singapore. Set kill conditions in advance, for example a review at ninety days if Light-to-Regular movement or new registrations fall sharply, so the paywall cannot become a permanent argument. Month-three churn remains unmeasured, but Option B is the only path that follows the evidence and can still be corrected.

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Pricing & Packaging

When to Charge

The option you are buying with free, the price of that option, and the moment the exchange rate turns against you.

Near-expert treatment. Assumes you already hold the working distinction between free-as-strategy and free-as-avoidance, the four-step timing procedure, and the arithmetic of cost-to-serve against burn.

1. Two decisions, three weeks apart

On the morning of 2 September 2026, in a low grey building on the Avinashi Road stretch outside Coimbatore, Devang Bhatt sat with a printout of a single row from his own cost ledger and could not make it stop being true. Bhatt runs Sorath Instruments, which makes the M3, a three-phase connected sub-meter that small and mid-sized manufacturers bolt onto a distribution board to see, for the first time, which machine on the shop floor is eating their electricity bill. The M3 sells for ₹18,400 at a 34% gross margin, which is to say ₹6,256 of gross profit per unit. Since 2022 every M3 has shipped with the Sorath cloud dashboard included, free, forever. There are 41,000 meters in the field, of which 26,800 report actively. Running the cloud for one active meter costs ₹62 a month. A meter stays in the field about six years. Sixty-two rupees times seventy-two months is ₹4,464 — seventy-one per cent of the gross margin on the hardware that carried it there, spent on a service the customer was told was free.

Bhatt's board had not asked him to raise prices. They had asked him a narrower and more awkward question: whether Sorath could name a single decision it had made differently because the dashboard was free. Four years of free had produced 41,000 installations, a respectable dealer network across Tamil Nadu, Gujarat and Maharashtra, and precisely zero observations of anyone paying anything for analytics. Sorath had been free for fifty months and had been learning for none of them.

Three weeks earlier and eight hundred kilometres north, on 8 September 2026, Meghna Sule opened a very different spreadsheet in a Baner conference room in Pune. Sule is VP Product at Sopaan Workforce Cloud, a five-year-old vertical SaaS company that sells attendance, shift rostering, statutory register maintenance and wage computation to factories, warehouses and third-party manpower contractors. Sopaan has 11,400 registered sites. Of these, 8,930 pay nothing, because the 2021 pricing page promised — in the word that would occupy the next four months of Sule's life — that Sopaan would be free forever for any site with forty workers or fewer. The remaining 2,470 sites pay an average of ₹11,500 a month, which is ₹34 crore of annualised revenue. Serving a free site costs ₹390 a month all-in: ₹85 of infrastructure, ₹230 of support, ₹75 of the quiet, unglamorous work of keeping Form-25 and Form-12 register templates current across nine state labour departments. Eight thousand nine hundred and thirty sites at ₹390 is ₹34.8 lakh a month, ₹4.18 crore a year, 12.3% of revenue.

Sule's problem was not that the number was large. It was that the number had grown every quarter for eleven quarters while the thing it was supposedly buying had not moved at all. Free-to-paid conversion, measured as an annualised rate over the last four quarters, ran 1.9%, 1.7%, 1.8%, 1.6%. The standard error on each of those estimates was about 0.14 percentage points. The estimates were, statistically, the same number four times. Sopaan was paying ₹1.05 crore a quarter to re-learn something it already knew to two decimal places.

These two companies look like they face the same decision and they do not. Sorath is uncertain and has bought no information. Sopaan is certain and keeps buying the same information anyway. The argument this page makes is that the difference between them — not the difference between free and paid, and not the difference between patience and avoidance as states of mind — is the whole of the topic, and that it can be made precise enough to referee an argument between two intelligent people who disagree.

2. The idea: free is not a price, it is a purchased option

Begin with a definition sharp enough to be wrong. To charge is to convert a unilateral transfer into a bilateral exchange; the timing question asks at what point the expected gain from the exchange exceeds the expected gain from the transfer. That formulation is deliberately austere, because it forces the two things most teams conflate into separate terms. The transfer has a gain — distribution, information, a defensive position, a standard in the market. The exchange has a gain — revenue, and, more importantly, the information revenue carries. Neither is zero. The decision is not "are we ready" but "which of these two streams is currently worth more per unit of time, and is the gap widening or narrowing."

Put more usefully for an operator: free is an option purchase. You are paying a recurring premium to hold open the right to decide later. The premium has three components, only one of which most teams carry on a ledger. The first is the marginal cost of service — infrastructure, support, the compliance work of keeping a free product legal — call it m × Nf, cost per free user times free base. The second is the reference-price accrual, which we will write as Γ: every month you are free, the market's belief that your product costs nothing hardens, and the eventual price you charge will be discounted, grandfathered or delayed by an amount that grows with the age and size of the free base. The third is organisational atrophy, Δ: a company that has never charged does not know how to charge, and the machinery of charging — billing, tax treatment, dunning, refunds, collections, sales compensation, revenue recognition — decays or was never built. Against this premium you receive one payoff: information, plus whatever distribution value the free base independently generates.

Monthly premium on the free option ≈ (m × Nf) + Γ + Δ
Monthly payoff ≈ value of information gained + value of distribution gained

The intellectual history of this question is older and messier than the freemium literature suggests, and knowing it prevents a specific class of error. The pre-history is retail loss-leading, in which a grocer prices flour below cost to sell everything else in the basket — a cross-subsidy inside one transaction. The story everybody tells, razors-and-blades, is largely false as history: Randal Picker's 2010 archival work showed that Gillette sold razors at a premium while its patents ran and only moved to cheap handles after the patents expired and imitators forced its hand. That matters here because the myth teaches that giving the durable away is a clever founding strategy, when the record shows it was a competitive concession made under duress. A great deal of "free as strategy" is the same concession told later as a plan.

Three genuine intellectual streams then converge. From economics came the formal result that below-cost pricing on one side of a market can be profit-maximising rather than charitable: Rochet and Tirole's 2003 work on two-sided platforms, and Parker and Van Alstyne's 2005 Management Science paper on two-sided network effects, established that when one group's participation raises another group's willingness to pay, the optimal price to the first group can be zero or negative, permanently and not as a phase. From behavioural economics came the finding that zero is not a point on a demand curve but a category of its own: Shampanier, Mazar and Ariely's 2007 experiments — the ones with the Hershey's Kiss and the Lindt truffle — showed demand jumping discontinuously at a price of zero in a way no smooth elasticity predicts. Thaler's earlier work on reference prices and transaction utility supplies the mechanism: a buyer evaluates a price against a remembered one, and the remembered price of a free product is zero. From the business-press and consulting side came the two poles that most practitioners have actually read — Chris Anderson's Free (2009), attacked with some force in Malcolm Gladwell's New Yorker review the same year, and the Simon-Kucher counter-tradition crystallised in Ramanujam and Tacke's Monetizing Innovation (2016). Sitting underneath all of it, and underused by product people, is decision analysis: Ronald Howard's 1966 information value theory, which gives the exact machinery for asking what a piece of evidence is worth before you buy it, and the real-options tradition from Dixit and Pindyck that prices the right to wait.

Those streams do not agree, and the disagreement is not decorative. Below is what each school will and will not sign. An expert can locate any argument about free inside this table within about ninety seconds, which is most of what refereeing a disagreement consists of.

Table 1 — Six positions on when to charge. Each is held by competent people. The right-hand columns are the discipline: a school is only real if there is something it refuses to say.
SchoolSigns thisRefuses to sign thisEvidence it rests on
Distribution
(Anderson; land-grab VC)		 Where a winner-takes-most equilibrium is plausible, the expected value of one more free user exceeds the revenue forgone from that user. That free is always cheaper than paid acquisition, or that scale reached at zero price is evidence of demand. Consumer internet 2004–2019; categories where the leader's share became unassailable before monetisation.
Monetisation-first
(Ramanujam / Simon-Kucher)		 A team that has never had a price conversation with a buyer does not yet know whether it has a product. That you must charge from day one. They allow free as a packaged element with a stated boundary; they forbid free as an absence of decision. Post-mortems of failed launches where the price conversation happened after the build.
Information / real options
(Howard; Dixit & Pindyck)		 Free is justified exactly when the expected value of the information it buys exceeds its premium, and no cheaper instrument yields the same information. That free is ever justified when the optimal action is the same whichever way the uncertainty resolves. Formal decision theory; internally consistent, rarely tested against messy field data.
Behavioural / reference price
(Ariely; Thaler)		 Demand is discontinuous at zero, and any later positive price is evaluated as a loss against a remembered zero. That the damage is permanent or unrecoverable. The effect is real; its half-life is contested. Laboratory price experiments; field evidence on price-increase churn is mixed and confounded.
Two-sided / platform
(Rochet & Tirole; Parker & Van Alstyne)		 Permanent zero or negative pricing on the side with the stronger cross-side externality can be the profit-maximising equilibrium, not a phase. That which side is "the free side" is obvious, fixed, or determined by who is more numerous. Formal models plus payment-card, media and marketplace history.
Cost-structure
(unit economics; the AI-era revision)		 Free is a licence granted only to businesses with near-zero and non-growing marginal cost, and a large class of products has just had that licence revoked. That cost determines price. It determines the feasibility of zero, which is a different claim. Inference, storage and egress cost curves; the observed convexity of usage distributions.

Notice what is not in the table: any school that holds "charge when the product is ready." That sentence survives in practice because it is unfalsifiable, and its persistence is the single most reliable marker of a team that has not thought about this. Readiness is not an observable. Cost, information and reference price all are.

3. Mechanics: pricing the option, and the test that collapses it

Expert practice has a shape, and it is not the four-step checklist. It is one calculation done properly and three corrections applied to it. The calculation is the value of information. The corrections are for saturation, selection and reversibility.

The calculation that decides everything

Howard's information value theory gives a quantity, the expected value of perfect information, with a property that turns out to be devastating in practice. Write the decision as a choice among actions a under uncertain states s with probabilities P(s) and payoffs U(a,s). Then:

EVPI = Σs P(s) · maxa U(a,s)  −  maxa Σs P(s) · U(a,s)

The first term is what you would earn if a reliable oracle told you the state before you acted. The second is what you earn acting on your current beliefs. The difference is the most any information about that uncertainty could possibly be worth. And here is the property: if the same action is optimal in every state you are uncertain about, the two terms are identical and EVPI is exactly zero. Not small. Zero. Waiting to resolve an uncertainty that does not change your action is not caution; it is, in the precise technical sense, buying something worth nothing.

Work it at Sopaan. Sule's team was genuinely uncertain about one thing: how a metered free tier would convert. They held two states in mind. State A: the free base is full of latent demand and a 40-worker cap, once it bites, converts 4% of free sites within a year. State B: the free base is full of genuinely tiny sites that will never pay, and metering converts 1.5%. Call them 35% and 65% likely, which is roughly where the room sat. The candidate actions were meter now and wait two quarters and re-look.

Under meter now in state A: 8,930 × 4% = 357 new paying sites at ₹11,500 a month, ₹41.1 lakh a month, ₹4.93 crore a year, less an assumed ₹0.6 crore of annualised support and discount friction, call it ₹4.33 crore net. Under meter now in state B: 134 sites, ₹15.4 lakh a month, ₹1.85 crore a year, less the same friction, ₹1.25 crore net. But metering also stops the bleeding: whichever state obtains, the free-tier cost line falls by roughly 70% as dormant sites lapse rather than convert, which is ₹2.9 crore a year recovered. So meter now is worth about ₹7.2 crore in state A and ₹4.15 crore in state B. Under wait, in both states, Sopaan earns nothing new and spends ₹2.09 crore over the two quarters of waiting, plus the Γ accrual on 8,930 sites growing older in their belief that Sopaan is free.

The optimal action is meter now in state A and meter now in state B. The uncertainty they had spent eleven quarters not resolving did not touch the decision. EVPI was zero. That is the rigorous restatement of "free as avoidance," and it is worth more than the slogan, because it is checkable by someone who disagrees with you. The question an expert asks is never "have we learned enough?" It is: name a result of this test that would make us do something different. If no one can, the test is not a test.

Now run the same machinery at Sorath and watch it give the opposite answer. Bhatt's uncertainty is the attach rate for a paid analytics SKU at ₹149 per meter per month. If attach is high — say 28% — the right action is a separate priced software product with its own roadmap, its own support motion and, eventually, its own P&L. If attach is low — say 8% — the right action is entirely different in kind: fold the analytics cost into the hardware price by raising the M3 by roughly ₹4,500, keep the dashboard free, and never build a software sales motion at all. Those are not two amounts of the same action. They are two different companies. The information genuinely flips the decision, so EVPI is large and positive, and a two-month attach probe run through eleven dealers in Gujarat is cheap at almost any price. Sorath should stay free a little longer and start charging some people immediately, which sounds contradictory only if you think the question is binary.

Correction one: information saturates on a square-root clock, and free bases are absurdly oversized for the question

The standard error of a proportion is √(p(1−p)/n). To halve a confidence interval you need four times the sample. This is arithmetic, and it has a consequence almost nobody draws. Suppose you want to know a conversion rate somewhere near 4% to within one percentage point at 95% confidence. Set 1.96√(0.04 × 0.96/n) = 0.01 and solve: n ≈ 1,476. Fifteen hundred users pushed through a real paywall answers the question. Sopaan's free base is 8,930 — six times the statistical requirement. Sonagiri Labs, a Hyderabad company we will meet shortly, has 128,000 free API keys, which is eighty-seven times the requirement and buys a precision of ±0.11 percentage points on a decision that does not change anywhere inside a two-point band.

Correction two: the free base measures the wrong population

Every estimate drawn from a free base is drawn from people who selected into a product at a price of zero. That population is systematically different from the population who would have selected in at ₹11,500 a month, and the difference runs in the direction that flatters you least: free bases over-represent the price-sensitive, the casually curious and the structurally unable-to-pay, and under-represent exactly the segment whose procurement process you need to learn. Sopaan's 8,930 free sites are, by construction, sites under forty workers — which in Indian manufacturing correlates with being unregistered for several of the compliance obligations Sopaan's paid product automates. The free base was not a smaller version of the paid market. It was a different market that happened to use the same software.

The correction is not statistical; it is instrumental. You do not de-bias a free cohort. You go and find the population you actually care about and expose them to a price. Sule's team eventually did this: they took 220 sites between 41 and 60 workers — just above the free ceiling, so never eligible for free, therefore never selected on price — and reconstructed their first-contact history. Those sites converted at 11.4%. The free base's 1.7% was not a fact about Sopaan's market. It was a fact about Sopaan's free tier.

Correction three: reversibility is asymmetric, so the first wall should be too tight

Loosening a limit costs nothing and generates goodwill. Tightening one costs a news cycle and a cohort. The expert consequence is counterintuitive: set the first paywall tighter than you believe is correct, and plan publicly to loosen it. A team that launches a ten-item free allowance and raises it to twenty-five after four weeks looks responsive. A team that launches at twenty-five and cuts to ten looks desperate, and every user who built a workflow at twenty-five is now a plaintiff. Docker's 2020 introduction of anonymous pull-rate limits and Slack's 2022 switch from a ten-thousand-message archive to a ninety-day window were both, technically, tightenings of a previously advertised free boundary, and both cost their companies weeks of public argument that a tighter original boundary would have avoided entirely.

The second-order effects nobody puts on the slide

Four consequences of free run through the organisation rather than the P&L, and they are where mature companies actually lose money. First, roadmap capture: a large free base generates the majority of feature requests, support tickets and app-store reviews, so the product organisation's attention drifts toward users who will never pay, and does so without anyone deciding it should. Second, competitive commitment: your free tier is a public, costly, hard-to-reverse signal that forecloses entry below you and simultaneously licenses entry above you — you have told every competitor exactly which price band is uncontested. Third, metric corruption: conversion rate, the headline number, has a denominator you control, so any team under pressure can improve it by shrinking the free base while making the business smaller. Fourth, and specific to India since 2023, regulatory surface: under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, consent, purpose limitation and erasure duties attach to a data fiduciary regardless of whether the data subject paid. A dormant free base of two lakh accounts is not a costless asset waiting to be monetised. It is a consent register you must maintain, a breach surface you must defend and an erasure obligation you must be able to execute.

Now the harder half: the circumstances in which this entire framing is actively misleading. There are four, and each has wrecked a competent team.

When the timing debate is a displaced packaging debate. A meeting that runs ninety minutes on "should we charge yet" and reaches no conclusion is usually a meeting in which two people hold incompatible views about the value metric and neither has said so. One believes the unit of value is the site; the other believes it is the worker. They cannot agree on when because they are pricing different products. The tell is that the discussion keeps returning to hypothetical customer objections rather than to cost or evidence. Send them away to agree on the metric and the timing question usually answers itself in ten minutes.

When the user is not the payer. In health, education, insurance distribution and anything sold to government, "should we charge the user" can be a category error. Free to the patient, paid by the hospital; free to the student, paid by the institution; free to the policyholder, paid by the insurer under whatever the current IRDAI distribution rules permit. The timing question here is about which counterparty's budget cycle you are entering and when their financial year turns, not about demand.

When one side of a multi-sided market is optimally free forever. If a genuine cross-side externality exists, treating zero as a temporary state to be outgrown is not patience or avoidance — it is a misunderstanding of the equilibrium. The failure mode is the reverse of the usual one: a new CFO looks at the free side, calls it unmonetised, and charges it.

When free is a procurement instrument rather than a price. This one is under-appreciated in India. Soham Grid Systems, which sells substation-monitoring software to state distribution utilities, ran free pilots at three DISCOMs for eighteen months in the belief that it was buying reference customers. What it was actually doing was creating a documented record of supply at zero, which a procurement officer is then obliged to reckon with when determining the reasonableness of rates in the subsequent tender. A prior free supply does not merely anchor the buyer psychologically; it enters the file. Sorath's dealers, similarly, are not psychologically anchored — they have a printed spec sheet listing the dashboard as included, and under the Consumer Protection Act framework an advertised inclusion is not a courtesy one can withdraw by changelog.

Multi-product: the internal transfer price nobody writes down

Sopaan has two modules. The statutory register module is free at every tier because it is what gets a factory manager to open the product at all; wage computation is paid. Internally, this is a cross-subsidy with no transfer price, which means the register team's costs sit in a line nobody defends and its wins accrue to a P&L it does not own. At the organisational seam, this always produces the same two pathologies: the free module is under-invested relative to its strategic role, and its true cost is invisible in every gross-margin conversation. The fix that mature companies use, and rarely admit to, is a synthetic internal transfer price — the free module "charges" the paid module a notional fee per activated site, so both appear in the ledger and both have an owner with something at stake. It is an accounting fiction and it changes behaviour immediately.

Two-sided: charging the side that is the product

Sopara Freight Systems, which matches shippers with return-load truck capacity out of Nhava Sheva and the Bhiwandi cluster, spent months fifteen to seventeen of its life charging fleet operators ₹1,200 a month for verified listing. Fleet-side supply fell 31% in six weeks. Shipper fill rate — the share of posted loads that got a confirmed truck — fell from 78% to 61%. Sopara had charged the scarce side, and in doing so degraded the exact thing the other side was there to buy. They rolled back; fill rate recovered to 81% within ten weeks. From month twenty-three they charged shippers ₹280 per confirmed booking and kept fleets permanently free. Bookings fell 8.3%, from 4,100 to 3,760 a month, and revenue went from nothing to ₹10.5 lakh a month. The general rule an expert carries: in a multi-sided market, charge the side whose participation is least elastic to price and least valuable to the other side per unit — and note that these are two different tests which usually, but not always, point the same way.

AI-native: the cost distribution, not the cost average

Sonagiri Labs sells a speech-to-text and speaker-diarisation API tuned for Indian languages and code-mixed audio. Its free tier offered 200 minutes a month per key. In September 2026 it had 128,000 free keys costing ₹1.14 crore a month in inference. The median free key used three minutes. The top 1,152 keys — nine-tenths of one per cent — consumed 46% of the spend, many of them by the simple expedient of registering new keys when the old one hit the ceiling. The instinct in the room was to cut the free allowance from 200 minutes to 60. The better move, which they took, was to change the shape of the free offer rather than its size: replace a recurring monthly allowance with a one-time credit grant worth about ₹500 of usage, and require a card on file for anything beyond it. Free-tier spend fell 61%, to ₹44 lakh a month. Weekly signups fell 4.2%, from 3,340 to 3,200. Paid conversion within sixty days of signup rose from 1.1% to 2.7%, because the card-on-file step is itself a selection instrument: it costs nothing and it separates intent from curiosity better than any survey.

Two AI-specific facts sit behind this. First, marginal cost is genuinely non-zero and, unlike bandwidth, has not yet been driven to irrelevance for the heaviest use. Second, and less discussed, the cost curve moves without you touching the product: upgrade the model and per-call cost changes, capability rises, sessions lengthen, and your free tier becomes more expensive with no decision having been made. A free tier defined in units of usage rather than in units of money re-prices itself against you every time the underlying stack improves. Sonagiri's credit grant is denominated in rupees precisely to close that hole.

What mature companies say versus what they do

Large companies say their free tier is a measured acquisition channel with a tracked lifetime value. What a great many of them actually run is a quarterly cost review in finance, an unannounced tightening of a limit, a hasty grandfathering of whichever cohort complains loudest, and a strategic narrative composed afterwards. The public record is full of the pattern: Evernote's 2016 restriction of free accounts to two devices, Heroku's 2022 retirement of free dynos, Unity's 2023 runtime fee announced, revised under pressure and cancelled a year later. None of these were irrational. All of them display the same signature — the free offer's boundary was set once, drifted for years without an owner, and was eventually corrected in a single visible jolt rather than adjusted continuously. The organisational lesson is that a free tier needs a named owner with a quarterly review and a mandate to move the boundary in small increments, or it will be moved in one large one by someone in finance who has never spoken to a user.

6. Ten things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: zero is a category, not a price, so the informative experiment is ₹1 and not ₹299. The competent practitioner tests a candidate price against free and learns the combined effect of "there is now a price" and "the price is ₹299." The expert separates them, because the demand discontinuity at zero — the Shampanier-Mazar-Ariely effect — swamps ordinary elasticity in the neighbourhood of zero. The tell-tale sign in the wild is a conversion test with exactly two cells, free and the target price. Running a token-price cell, even one that loses money, isolates how much of the churn is about money and how much is about the act of asking. Sohbat Care, later in this page, would have been saved a year by that one extra cell.

Two: the information clock starts at the first price test, not at launch. This is the mistake Fig. 1 is drawn to make visible. Teams say "we have been learning for four years" when what they mean is "we have been operating for four years." Sorath had 41,000 installations and not one observation of price. The tell-tale sign is a team that can quote usage statistics to three significant figures and cannot state a single number about willingness to pay that was not self-reported. The obvious reading — that a big base implies rich evidence — is wrong because usage evidence and price evidence are different measurements, and only one of them requires you to have asked.

Three: the free base measures a population selected on the very variable you are trying to estimate. The competent practitioner computes conversion from the free base and reports it as the market's conversion rate. The expert treats it as a lower bound contaminated by selection, and goes looking for a never-free cohort — customers just above the free ceiling, inbound leads who never signed up, a geography where free was never offered. Sopaan's never-free 41-to-60-worker sites converted at 11.4% against the free base's 1.7%. The tell-tale sign is a pricing deck whose every number has the same denominator.

Four: "forever" is a liability with a net present value, and someone should compute it. Most teams treat the marketing copy of three years ago as a communications problem. It is a balance-sheet item. The tell-tale sign that you are dealing with an expert is that they ask to see the archived pricing page and the terms of service before they ask to see the cohort data, and that they know to ask which cohort signed up while the strongest version of the promise was live.
