Six: the cost of free is convex in the tail, so the right instrument is a cap, not a price. The competent practitioner reads the mean cost per free user and finds it tolerable. The expert asks for the distribution and discovers, as Sonagiri did, that a fraction of a per cent of accounts is most of the bill. The tell-tale sign is a cost-per-free-user figure quoted without a percentile. The consequence of the distinction is that the correct first action is frequently not to introduce a price at all — it is to cap the tail, which preserves the entire strategic benefit of free while removing most of its cost, and buys you the time to make the pricing decision properly rather than under duress.

Seven: a free tier is a competitive commitment, and commitments cut both ways. The competent practitioner thinks of free as defensive. The expert reads it as a public announcement of which price band is uncontested and looks at who entered afterwards. If a rival launched at ₹6,000 a month eighteen months after you went free below forty workers, your free tier did not deter them — it told them where to stand. The tell-tale sign is a competitive landscape where every new entrant is priced above you and none below. The obvious reading, that this proves your free tier works, is exactly backwards: you have ceded the premium end and made yourself the reference for cheap.

Eight: conversion rate is a ratio whose denominator you control, and therefore a corruptible objective. Any team told to improve free-to-paid conversion can do so by making the free tier worse, smaller or harder to reach, shrinking the denominator while shrinking the business. The expert watches absolute paid additions and revenue per free user, and treats a rising conversion rate alongside falling absolute adds as a red flag rather than a win. The tell-tale sign is a growth review in which conversion percentage is on the slide and the count of new paying accounts is not.

Nine: "we'll monetise later" is a prediction about a future team, and it is almost always wrong in the same direction. The team that inherits the decision will face a larger free base, an older and harder reference price, a weaker billing capability and, on average, a worse funding environment. The expert's diagnostic is a single question asked without irony: what will be easier about this decision in twelve months? A specific, credible answer — "our enterprise tier will exist, so free users will have somewhere to go" — is a reason to wait. Silence, or a general appeal to more data, is the answer. The tell-tale sign is that the same slide appears in four consecutive quarterly reviews with the date changed.

Ten: do not change more than one thing at once, because the cost of an unattributable outcome is the whole experiment. The competent practitioner, under board pressure, launches the paywall alongside the redesign and the new tier structure, reasoning that the disruption should be absorbed in one go. The expert knows that the point of the launch is not the revenue, which will be small, but the learning, which will be the basis of the next three years of pricing — and that three simultaneous changes destroy attribution completely. The tell-tale sign is a launch plan with more than one large change in the same fortnight and no holdout group. The cost of catching this late is that you cannot diagnose your own failure, which is precisely what happened at Sohbat Care.

7. How it differs by product type and stage — and where it does not

In consumer products the binding constraint is the value-accrual arc: the interval between first use and the moment a user could sincerely say the product matters. In a photo app that interval is minutes; in mental health, language learning or fitness it is eight to fourteen weeks. A trial shorter than the arc prices a product the user has not yet experienced, which is why the seven-day trial is the single most over-used instrument in consumer software. The correct wall for a long-arc product is not temporal at all but behavioural — after the fourth completed week, after the tenth session, after the habit exists.

In B2B and enterprise the constraint is the buying calendar and the champion's internal case, and fully free is rarer than it looks because what is usually called free is a pilot with an unenforced end date. The timing question becomes: does the champion have a number to take to their finance partner, and does the buying window open before or after your cash does? The specifically enterprise trap is channel conflict — a free tier that lets a business unit start without procurement will eventually collide with the account executive whose quota depends on procurement being involved. That collision is organisational, not analytical, and it is resolved by compensation design or it is not resolved.

In platforms and marketplaces the question is not when but which side, and the answer can be permanent. Sopara's fleets will be free for as long as return-load capacity is the scarce input. The discipline required is to re-test the scarcity assumption annually rather than to treat the free side as sacred, because scarcity migrates.

In hardware and physical goods the revenue event is discrete and the cost event is continuous, so the real question is whether the attached service is a margin leak or a second product — and the installed base makes the decision partly irreversible the moment the first unit ships with an advertised inclusion. Sorath's six-year overhang is the general case, not a peculiarity.

In AI products two things are genuinely new and one thing widely claimed is not. Genuinely new: marginal cost is material at the tail, and the cost curve moves without a product decision when the model underneath changes. Not new: the claim that AI makes the timing question different in kind. It does not. It moves the crossover in Fig. 1 substantially to the left, which is a change in magnitude, and it makes usage-denominated free offers dangerous, which is a change in instrument design. The analysis is the same analysis.

By stage, the honest differences are narrower than the literature suggests. Early companies have small bases and weak reference prices, so their free decisions are cheap to reverse and their information is expensive to obtain; late companies have the opposite. Early companies should therefore test prices early and often on small samples; late companies should move boundaries continuously and in small increments rather than in one visible jolt.

Where there is no real difference worth teaching: information saturates on the same square-root clock in every product type; the billing capability atrophies at the same rate in a marketplace as in a hardware company; the cost distribution is convex in the tail everywhere anyone has bothered to look; and in every category the question "what result would change our action" separates the teams who are learning from the teams who are waiting. Claims that consumer pricing and enterprise pricing are fundamentally different disciplines are usually claims about sales motion dressed up as claims about pricing.

8. Three worked examples

Sopara Freight Systems: charging the right side, eventually

Sopara's numbers are worth stating as a sequence because the sequence is the lesson. Months 1–14: both sides free, 6,200 verified fleet operators, 11,900 trucks, 1,840 shippers, 4,100 bookings a month, fill rate 78%. Months 15–17: ₹1,200 a month charged to fleets. Fleet-side active supply −31%; fill rate 78% → 61%; shipper posting volume −19% as a consequence, because a shipper who cannot get a truck stops posting. Revenue from the fleet fee: ₹18.6 lakh over three months. Revenue destroyed on the shipper side, measured as forgone bookings at the eventual take rate: considerably more, and the fill-rate damage took ten weeks to repair after the rollback. Months 23 onward: ₹280 per confirmed booking charged to shippers; bookings 4,100 → 3,760 (−8.3%); revenue ₹10.5 lakh a month and growing with volume rather than fixed. The instructive arithmetic is the elasticity comparison: fleets showed a 31% quantity response to a fee worth about 4% of their monthly revenue; shippers showed an 8.3% response to a fee worth about 1.8% of freight cost. Same platform, same month, elasticities differing by a factor of four.

Sonagiri Labs: changing the shape of free rather than its size

Covered above in the AI edge case, but the counterfactual deserves a line. Sonagiri modelled the instinctive move — cutting the monthly allowance from 200 minutes to 60 — and projected a 58% cost reduction with a 19% fall in signups, because the allowance cut degrades the experience of the median free key, which uses three minutes and is entirely unaffected by the tail's behaviour. The credit-grant design achieved a 61% cost reduction with a 4.2% signup fall by targeting the tail specifically. The difference between a 19% and a 4.2% signup decline is not a rounding error; at Sonagiri's volumes it is roughly 2,300 developers a quarter, and developer adoption compounds. The instrument mattered more than the magnitude.

Sohbat Care: the failure, and what recovery actually cost

Sohbat Care is a Bengaluru consumer application offering guided journaling, structured cognitive-behavioural exercises and, latterly, therapist matching. From January 2023 to February 2026 it was entirely free, with no ads and no tier. It reached 2,74,000 monthly active users and a 4.6 app-store rating. In February 2026, with eight months of runway, it launched a hard paywall: everything behind ₹499 a month after a seven-day trial. It launched this simultaneously with a complete visual redesign and a new three-tier package including therapist sessions.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Roadmap capture. Early sign: in the last ten shipped features, the requesting cohort was free for seven or more. Diagnostic question: which paying customer asked for this? Cost of catching it late: two years of engineering spent on a population that will never pay, and a paid product that has visibly stopped improving, which shows up first as flat expansion revenue.

Grandfathering debt. Early sign: more than three distinct legacy price cohorts live in the billing system. Diagnostic question: how many price points can we currently bill, and what would it cost to retire one? Cost of catching it late: every subsequent pricing change requires a migration project, and the finance team begins to veto pricing changes on operational grounds — which is how a company loses the ability to price at all.

Tail-cost blowout. Early sign: total free-tier cost grows faster than free-user count for two consecutive quarters. Diagnostic question: what is the 99th-percentile cost per free account, and is the gap to the median widening? Cost of catching it late: a cost line that has become material enough to force an abrupt, visible restriction — the Docker and Heroku pattern.

The unattributable launch. Early sign: a launch plan with two or more significant changes in the same window and no holdout. Diagnostic question: if this goes badly, what will we know? Cost of catching it late: the full price of the experiment with none of the learning, as at Sohbat.

Capability gap. Early sign: nobody can name the owner of the billing system in under ten seconds. Diagnostic question: from a decision this afternoon, what date do we collect? Cost of catching it late: the tripwire fires and nothing happens for four months, which in a cash crunch is the whole game.

Compliance surprise. Early sign: the pricing plan has no line for GST place-of-supply treatment, e-invoicing, e-mandate pre-debit notification or app-store billing share. Diagnostic question: who has read the current terms, and what did the archived pricing page actually promise? Cost of catching it late: a launch date slipping by six to ten weeks at precisely the moment the slip is most expensive, plus the possibility that the promise you made in 2021 is enforceable.

Charging the scarce side. Early sign: a multi-sided product where the side being asked to pay is the one the other side is actually shopping for. Diagnostic question: if this side halved, what would happen to the other side's retention? Cost of catching it late: liquidity collapse, which repairs on a ten-to-twenty-week timescale if it repairs at all.

The mean-cost illusion. Early sign: any sentence of the form "free costs us about X per user." Diagnostic question: show me the histogram. Cost of catching it late: pricing the body of the distribution to solve a problem that lives entirely in its tail, which is the one error that makes both the cost and the growth worse at the same time.

10. Where competent experts genuinely disagree

Does the zero reference price actually persist? The behavioural position, steelmanned: demand is measurably discontinuous at zero, the endowment effect makes withdrawal feel like loss rather than forgone gain, and any later price is judged against a remembered zero rather than against value — so every month of free raises the price of leaving free, non-linearly. It rests on clean laboratory evidence. The empirical counter-position, steelmanned: the field record shows a great many bases moved from zero to positive with churn in the 10–25% range and revenue up sharply, and what predicts damage is the manner of the change — notice, grandfathering, whether the wall matches the value arc — not the existence of a prior zero. It rests on the observed outcomes of dozens of freemium transitions. For the behavioural position to be wrong, you would need matched bases, one previously free and one not, converted under identical terms, showing no difference; nobody has run that experiment, and survivorship bias in the field record cuts hard, because the companies destroyed by their paywalls do not write case studies.

Is a free tier actually a cheap acquisition channel? For, steelmanned: the fully loaded cost of a free signup approaches infrastructure cost, referrals from free users are genuinely free, and in developer and prosumer categories the free tier is the only channel that reaches the person who chooses the tool. Against, steelmanned: "free CAC" is almost always computed excluding the cost of servicing the free base and excluding the conversion-rate dilution from low-intent signups, and when those are loaded in, free-tier CAC in many categories is comparable to paid CAC with materially worse cohort quality. What would settle it: the referral coefficient from free users. Above roughly 0.3 the "for" case is overwhelming; Sopaan measured 0.06, which makes its free tier an expensive channel wearing a cheap costume. Most companies have never measured it.

Has AI permanently changed the rule, or is this a transient cost curve? Permanently, steelmanned: marginal cost per interaction is bounded below by energy and silicon, and capability improvements induce deeper usage rather than cheaper usage — a Jevons dynamic — so the cost per engaged free user may not fall even as cost per token does. Transient, steelmanned: cost per token has fallen by orders of magnitude in a handful of years and there is no reason to believe it has stopped; a company that redesigns its business around today's inference price is making the same mistake as a company that redesigned around 2001 bandwidth prices. For the "permanent" case to be wrong, cost per completed user task — not per token — would have to fall materially, and the honest position is that this is measurable and almost nobody is measuring it.

Should one side of a multi-sided market be permanently free? The formal result says yes, where the cross-side externality is strong enough. The practitioner objection is not that the model is wrong but that the optimality claim is asserted once at founding and never re-tested, while the free side accretes internal constituency — a team, a metric, a vice-president — that makes re-testing politically impossible. Both sides of this argument are right, which is why the workable rule is procedural rather than substantive: re-derive which side is scarce every year, in writing, with numbers.

Price before product, or product before price? Ramanujam's position is that the willingness-to-pay conversation must precede the build, and its evidence is a long tail of technically excellent products that nobody would pay for. The discovery-school counter is that in genuinely new categories, buyers cannot price what they have not experienced, and early price conversations systematically under-estimate willingness to pay for things that turn out to be indispensable. Both cite real cases. The reconciliation people reach for — "do both" — is not actually available in a seed-stage company with eleven people, which is why this disagreement is live rather than academic.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in ways an observer can see. They keep a written premium ledger for the free tier, with the three components separated, reviewed quarterly by a named owner. Asked why the product is free, they give one of three answers — distribution, information, or a cross-side externality — and can produce the measurement behind it rather than the intention. They size a free base to the statistical question rather than to ambition, and are comfortable saying that fifteen hundred exposed users is enough. They ask, of every proposed delay, what result would change the action, and they treat the absence of an answer as a decision rather than as an open question. They design the first paywall too tight on purpose. They refuse to bundle the timing change with a packaging change or a redesign, even when the calendar is against them, because they know the learning is worth more than the quarter. They know their days-to-first-rupee number without looking it up. They read the archived pricing page before the cohort data. They look at the cost distribution rather than the cost mean, and reach for a cap before a price. They treat grandfathering as debt, with a schedule and a retirement plan. And they are equally willing to say the two sentences that most teams can only say one of: free is correct here, permanently, and here is the externality that makes it so, and we have been avoiding this for six quarters and the evidence stopped moving in 2024.

12. What Sule and Bhatt decided

Meghna Sule did not launch a price. On 26 September 2026 she capped the free tier — fifteen worker-records synced per day, unlimited register access — which is a tail cap, not a wall, and which required no notice period because it restricted a rate rather than withdrawing a promise. Simultaneously she started the 118-day billing and legal track shown in Fig. 4, and ran a metered paid test on 1,500 free sites selected at random, with a 1,500-site holdout and a ₹1-per-site token cell to separate the shock of being charged from the level of the charge. The 6,100 "free forever" sites were excluded from the test and moved to the feature-boundary path in Table 3: everything Sopaan shipped before October 2026 remains free for them permanently, everything after is paid. The reasoning she gave the board was the EVPI argument in plain words: the conversion number has not moved in eleven quarters and would not change what we do at any plausible value, so we are not waiting for information, we are waiting. The one thing we genuinely do not know is what the never-free segment above the ceiling will pay, and that costs nine lakh to find out.

Devang Bhatt made almost the opposite decision for the same reason. Sorath kept the dashboard free for all 41,000 installed meters, permanently and in writing, because the promise was made at point of sale and because Table 4 showed the legacy overhang decaying on its own six-year clock. From 1 November 2026 the M3 ships with basic readings free and a ₹149-per-month "Insight" tier, sold through eleven dealers in Gujarat only, for ninety days, with attach rate as the single measured outcome. If attach clears 22%, Sorath builds a software business and hires for it. If it comes in under 12%, Sorath raises the M3 by ₹4,500, keeps analytics free forever, and stops pretending to be a software company. Bhatt's board found the second branch uncomfortable, which is the sign that it was a real experiment: a test whose losing outcome you have not agreed to accept is not a test.

Discussion questions.

1. Sule excluded the 6,100 "free forever" sites from her paid test in order to avoid a legal exposure, and in doing so removed the largest and oldest cohort from the evidence base. Was the resulting estimate worth having? What would you have done instead, and what would it have cost?

2. Bhatt committed in advance to raising hardware prices and abandoning the software plan if attach came in under 12%. Sopaan's board made no such pre-commitment. Which board governed better, and does your answer depend on knowing how the tests turned out?

3. Sohbat Care's recovery produced a real business at a permanently lower blended price. Suppose you had been in the room in January 2026 and had been overruled on sequencing. At what point, and on what evidence, would you have been entitled to say the paywall itself was not the mistake?

13. Going deeper

Revenue models
Upstream of everything here: the model determines whether a user-facing price exists at all, and an advertising or insurer-funded model makes the whole timing question a category error. Unlocks the ability to tell a genuine two-sided free from an unexamined one.
Willingness-to-pay probes in interviews
The cheapest instrument in Table 2's C6 test, and the one most often mis-run. Matters next because a well-designed probe on a never-free population is worth more than two years of free-base telemetry.
Willingness-to-pay research
Van Westendorp, Gabor-Granger and conjoint give you a demand curve rather than a point, which is what turns the timing decision into a pricing decision. Unlocks the ability to price the option in Fig. 1 rather than merely to notice it.
The value metric
Most unresolvable timing arguments are value-metric arguments in disguise, as section 4 argued. Settling the metric — per site, per worker, per meter, per minute — usually collapses the timing debate immediately.
Packaging: good / better / best
Timing tells you when to open the door; packaging decides how many rooms lie behind it and who is routed to which. Unlocks the ability to charge without withdrawing, which is how the reference-price problem is usually defused in practice.
Freemium vs free trial
The instrument choice that Sohbat got wrong and Sonagiri got right. Matters next because the shape of a free offer determines its cost distribution and its reversibility far more than its size does.
What pricing signals
A price is a claim about what kind of product this is and who it is for. Relevant here because the decision to charge is also the decision to stop being the free option in your category, with the competitive consequences described in nuance seven.
AI cost-to-serve and pricing
The direct continuation of the Sonagiri material: how to measure cost per completed task rather than per token, and how to build offers that do not re-price themselves against you when the model underneath changes.
